html:
In October 539 BCE the Persian king Cyrus the Great defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris, and days later his troops entered Babylon, it seems without a fight. It ended the Neo-Babylonian Empire, the last great empire ruled from Mesopotamia by native kings.

Babylon's king Nabonidus had made enemies at home. He favoured the moon god Sin over Babylon's own god Marduk and spent ten years away at an oasis in Arabia, leaving his son Belshazzar in charge. Cyrus presented himself as Marduk's chosen king who had come to restore proper worship, a message spread by the Cyrus Cylinder. The Book of Daniel tells of Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall on the night the city fell, and Herodotus says the Persians entered along a river bed they had drained.

Babylon stayed a great city, now a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Cyrus let deported peoples go home, among them the Jews of the exile, starting the Return to Zion.
